stories.title: When Grandma Takes Many Different Medicines
stories.headline_kid: Did you know some grandparents in Singapore take more than 5 different medicines every single day?
summary: Many older people in Singapore need several kinds of medicine to stay healthy — for things like high blood pressure, diabetes or joint pain. In fact, about 1 in 7 seniors above 66 years old take more than five different prescription medicines every day, according to a Singapore health survey.

The tricky part is that when someone takes many medicines together, it becomes hard to tell which one is causing a side effect, like feeling dizzy or sleepy. It's a bit like drinking five different fruit juices at once — if your tummy feels funny afterwards, how would you know which juice caused it?

That's why family members who look after grandparents need to be extra careful. Doctors suggest keeping a clear list of every medicine, setting reminders so nothing is missed, and asking the pharmacist questions whenever something new is added.
This story is a gentle reminder to check in on our grandparents and elderly relatives — asking how they're feeling can help catch problems early, long before they become serious.

lenses.me: You could help by reminding a grandparent to take their pills on time, or by simply asking them how they feel each day.
lenses.family: Families who care for elderly relatives need to track many medicines carefully to keep them safe from mix-ups.
lenses.friends: Classmates who live with grandparents might share this same responsibility at home.
lenses.nation: As Singapore's population grows older, more families will need to learn how to manage medicines safely.
lenses.world: Countries everywhere are facing the same challenge as people live longer and take more medicines.

stories.title: Ferry Fire Tragedy Near the Philippines
stories.headline_kid: A ferry near the Philippines caught fire days ago, and rescuers are still finding out what happened to everyone on board.
summary: A passenger ferry called the M/V June Aster caught fire near Palawan, a group of islands in the Philippines that many tourists visit. The fire happened several days ago, and as rescue workers searched the burnt ship, they sadly found more bodies — bringing the total number of deaths to 76.

The coast guard has been carefully bringing the remains to a nearby town. Because the fire made it hard to recognise people straight away, temporary graves have been dug so doctors can carry out DNA tests to work out who each person was.
Officials are still investigating why the fire started in the first place. Some passengers had to jump into the sea to escape the flames and smoke.

The Philippines is a popular holiday spot for many Singaporean families, so this sad news is a good reminder of why we should always listen carefully to safety briefings before any boat or plane trip.

lenses.me: Think about the safety talks you hear before a flight or ferry ride — they matter more than you might think.
lenses.family: If your family is planning a trip to the Philippines, this news might make them double-check travel safety.
lenses.friends: Friends who have visited or have relatives in the Philippines may feel worried by this news.
lenses.nation: Singapore often offers help to neighbouring countries during such disasters, showing regional friendship.
lenses.world: This tragedy highlights why sea travel safety rules are so important across Southeast Asia.

stories.title: Malaysian Party's Idea to Reserve Government Jobs Sparks Debate
stories.headline_kid: A political party in Malaysia wants only Muslims to hold top government jobs — and many people are unhappy about it.
summary: Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS), an Islamic political party in Malaysia, has suggested that Cabinet positions — the top jobs in the government — should be reserved only for Muslim politicians. This idea has caused a lot of debate across the country.

A lawmaker called the proposal 'divisive', meaning it could split people apart instead of bringing them together. A group representing different religions also said the idea might go against Malaysia's constitution, the country's most important set of rules, which promises fair treatment for people of every faith.

This isn't the first time PAS has made such a suggestion. Critics say the party keeps pushing for Malaysia to become more of an Islamic state, which worries citizens who follow other religions, such as Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism.

Malaysia is Singapore's closest neighbour, and many Singaporeans have relatives and friends there. This story is a good reminder of why Singapore works so hard to make sure people of every race and religion are treated fairly and feel they belong.

lenses.nation: This story shows why Singapore's own policies, like Racial Harmony Day, matter so much to keep our society fair.
lenses.world: It reflects a bigger debate happening in many countries about religion and government.

stories.title: China Grows Its Own King of Fruits
stories.headline_kid: Farmers on a Chinese island are using clever technology to grow durians — could this change how much durian costs in Singapore?
summary: Hainan, a tropical island in China, is trying something new: growing durian, the spiky, smelly-but-tasty fruit many Singaporeans love, sometimes called the 'king of fruits'.

It's not easy, though. Hainan gets hit by typhoons (very strong storms), durian trees take many years before they produce fruit, and farmers there only have small pieces of land — so they can't grow anywhere near as much durian as Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia.
Instead of trying to grow huge amounts, Hainan's farmers are using technology and careful farming methods to grow smaller amounts of premium, top-quality durian that can be sold at higher prices.

Singapore gets most of its durians from Malaysia and Thailand. If China becomes a new durian producer, durian lovers here might one day have even more choices — and maybe even new flavours — at the supermarket or when ordering durian delivery.

stories.title: Singapore's Darren Yap Kicks Off in a Brand-New Sport
stories.headline_kid: A cool new sport that mixes taekwondo and video games is making its debut at the Asian Games — and a Singaporean is competing!
summary: At the 2026 Asian Games, a brand-new event called virtual taekwondo is being held for the very first time. Athletes wear sensors that track their kicks and punches, and their moves appear on a screen just like a fighting video game.
Singapore's Darren Yap will represent our country in two events: poomsae, a traditional taekwondo pattern event, and this exciting new virtual taekwondo event.

You might think virtual taekwondo sounds easy because it looks like a video game — but Darren says it's actually really tough. The sensors are strict about correct technique, so athletes still need excellent form, speed and fitness to score points.
This new sport shows how technology and traditional sports are coming together, giving young Singaporeans an exciting new way to get involved in martial arts.
